extracted.intended_audience: poets, writers, painters, architects, rhetoricians, and artists interested in producing or analysing the sublime
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical guidance for producing the aesthetic effect of the sublime across arts (poetry, painting, architecture, sound), emphasising terror, power, vastness, privation, light/dark, and related devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terror as the common stock of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Terror is the fundamental emotion underpinning the sublime; many causes of the sublime rise naturally from terror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the audience with solemnity and apprehension before revealing the cause; the sense of being terrified heightens the sublime effect. Example: a vision presented after a solemn and terrifying prelude will be felt as more sublime. Anti-pattern: presenting the grand cause too clearly or without prior solemn preparation reduces its power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power (modification of the sublime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power, in its various forms, is a primary source of the sublime; the idea of vast power is closely linked with terror and awakens awe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict power as potentially injurious or unconstrained to evoke sublimity—strength that threatens rather than serves. Examples and contrasts: an ox (innocent, subservient) is not sublime; a bull or a free, fiercer horse is. Institutional power (sovereigns, commanders) also produces awe. Anti-pattern: stripping power of its ability to hurt (making it purely useful/subservient) converts it into contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association of pain>pleasure (psychological asymmetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind is more strongly affected by ideas of pain and death than by pleasure; when chances for suffering and enjoyment are equal, the idea of suffering prevails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit this asymmetry by emphasizing danger, pain, or death when seeking a grand effect. Use imagery that suggests the capacity to inflict suffering to maintain terror. This underpins why power tends to be sublime: because it implies the capacity to inflict pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity and the limits of painting vs. poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscure, incomprehensible, or fantastic apparitions are often rendered better in poetry than in painting; literal visual depiction risks ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language and suggested images that preserve obscurity and incomprehensibility (allegory, chimeras, ambiguous apparitions) rather than forcing literal, detailed visual representation. Anti-pattern: assembling too many explicit, literal phantoms in visual art can become grotesque or ludicrous; keep some things wrapped in darkness or ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privation: vacuity, darkness, solitude, silence
rubrics_metrics.description: General privations (vacuity, darkness, solitude, silence) are powerful causes of the sublime because they are terrible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke emptiness, silence, solitude, or darkness to create a sense of dread and the sublime—e.g., Virgil's depiction of the mouth of hell. Use absence as a substantive device rather than merely a background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vastness and greatness of dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness of dimension (length, height, depth) is a powerful cause of the sublime; certain modes of extension produce stronger effects than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer height/depth and perpendiculars over mere length; rugged, broken surfaces are stronger than smooth ones. When describing or constructing large things, emphasize those aspects that make them seem immeasurable. Consider that depth (looking down from a precipice) often strikes more than length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity (actual or apparent) as a sublime source
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinity fills the mind with a 'delightful horror'—objects that seem without bounds (real or apparent) produce the most genuine sublime effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create impressions of infinite extension (actual infinity is rare in senses) by repeating elements or arranging parts so that the imagination meets no natural check. Use devices that prevent the mind from finding bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession and uniformity (artificial infinity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial infinity requires (1) succession—parts continuing in one direction—and (2) uniformity—unchanging parts so the imagination is not checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated, uniform elements (e.g., rows of pillars, long aisles, rotundas) to give the impression of endless continuation. Avoid alterations in figure, disposition, or color that interrupt the succession. Architectural caution: cross-shaped plans introduce directional breaks that destroy the progressive illusion; prefer continuous colonnades or rotund forms for the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude in building (proportion and deceptive design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large dimensions are necessary for architectural sublimity, but sheer length without proportion can destroy grandeur; perspective can reduce perceived height if length is excessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balanced medium between excessive and insufficient dimensions. Use 'generous deceit' (design techniques that make buildings feel larger than they are) rather than mere enormous size. Avoid extremely long colonnades or avenues that run to impracticable distances; moderate lengths often appear grander.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity in pleasing objects (the attractiveness of incompleteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A kind of pleasant infinity arises in agreeable objects when they promise more—unfinished or suggestive works (young plants, sketches) please by entertaining the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking pleasure rather than terror, preserve a sense of promise or incompletion to engage the imagination (e.g., unfinished sketches, young life). Don't overfinish if you want to preserve imaginative engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty (labour and force displayed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appearance that immense force and labor were required to produce a work is itself a source of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize toil, effort, and the massive difficulty behind works to magnify their grandeur. Roughness or rudeness (as in Stonehenge) can increase sublimity because it excludes ideas of delicate contrivance and emphasizes brute force. Anti-pattern: overly refined dexterity produces a different (non-sublime) effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence (profusion and multitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: A great profusion of splendid or valuable things, when it produces an appearance of almost infinite abundance, is magnificent and can be sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use large number and apparent disorder (when it suggests infinity) to dazzle the imagination—e.g., starry heaven, rich poetic enumerations. Exercise caution: profusion can destroy usefulness and taste if it is merely disorderly; only admit this device where splendour is the aim (fireworks, grand panegyrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Light: extremes, transitions, and contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Light affects the sublime: extreme light (sun) or rapid transitions between light and darkness produce grandeur; darkness often more productive of sublime than ordinary light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ extreme light or rapid light–dark contrasts to overpower the senses (e.g., lightning, the sun). Use darkness deliberately—'With majesty of darkness round / Circles his throne'—to surround the incomprehensible. Recognize that excessive light can function like darkness by obliterating objects (blindness effect). Avoid middling illumination when aiming for the highest effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light in building (prefer gloom for the sublime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Edifices intended to produce sublime impressions should tend toward darkness and gloom rather than bright illumination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interior lighting to create a striking transition from external brightness to interior gloom (by day); at night, the converse holds—high illumination then produces grandeur. Use darkness to heighten solemnity and awe; only use bright, cheerful light where a different effect is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color for the sublime (melancholy hues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft, cheerful colors are unfit for producing grand images; melancholy, fuscous colors (black, brown, deep purple) contribute to the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In painting or architectural materials intended for the sublime, avoid white, green, yellow, blue, pale red, violet, or spotted colors; favor somber tones. Use gilding, mosaics, and brilliant ornament sparingly—these often detract from the highest sublimity. Caveat: this rule applies mainly when a uniform, consistent degree of striking sublimity is required; in other edifices draw on other sources of grandeur but avoid 'light and riant' elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound and loudness
rubrics_metrics.description: Loud, overwhelming sounds (cataracts, storms, thunder, artillery, the shout of multitudes) produce great and awful sensations akin to the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use powerful, loud sonic phenomena to overpower and astonish—sound alone (even without nicety or musical artifice) can fill the mind with terror and grandeur. For communal effects, the noise of crowds can sweep individuals into collective resolution or awe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness (abrupt onset or cessation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden beginning or cessation of a strong sound rouses attention and produces terror; sudden transitions stir the faculties and can be sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ abrupt starts or stops (single strong sounds, gun salutes with pauses, a great clock striking in the night) to startle and elevate the imagination. Avoid easy transitions between extremes if you want to create terror—the smooth transitions kill the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermitting (low, tremulous, uncertain sounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Low, tremulous, intermitting, or uncertain sounds can be more alarming than total silence because they leave causes uncertain and provoke fearful imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit uncertain, intermittent sounds (faint distant noises, fading hammers, flickering light accompanied by sound) to sustain anxiety and dread. Combine with darkness or obscurity to heighten the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural cries and animal tones
rubrics_metrics.description: Sounds imitating natural, inarticulate voices of men or animals in pain or danger, or the angry tones of wild beasts, effectively convey great ideas and sublime sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural cries and animalistic sounds (real or imitated) rather than articulate language to convey primal terror; such modulations are universally intelligible and carry a direct connection with the nature of the things they represent. Anti-pattern: familiar, contemptible voices (e.g., those of domesticated animals used in familiar contexts) fail to produce sublimity.
